'''''Rubus occidentalis''''' is a species of [[bramble]] native to eastern North America. Its [[common name]] '''black raspberry''' is shared with [[black raspberry|other closely related species]]. Other names include '''bear's eye blackberry''', '''black cap''', '''black cap raspberry''',<ref name="grin">{{GRIN | access-date = 19 July 2025}}</ref><ref>Michigan Bee Plants: [http://plants.bees.net/gallery/view_photo.php?set_albumName=rubus&id=Rubus_occidentalis_fig_2_CRW_2542_RT8 ''Rubus occidentalis'']</ref> and '''scotch cap'''.<ref>Britton, N.L.; Brown, A. 1897. ''An illustrated flora of the Northern United States, Canada and the British possessions from Newfoundland to the parallel of the Southern boundary of Virginia, and from the Atlantic Ocean westward to the 102d meridian''. Charles Scribner's Sons, New York.</ref>

==Description==
''Rubus occidentalis'' is a [[deciduous]] shrub growing to {{convert|2 to 3|m|ft|frac=2|spell=in|abbr=off}} tall.<ref name="marrone">{{Cite book|last=Marrone|first=Teresa|title=Indiana, Kentucky and Ohio Wild Berries & Fruits Field Guide|publisher=Adventure Publications, Inc|year=2011|page=262|isbn=9781591933069}}</ref> Immature [[Plant stem|stems]], also called canes, are unbranched and have a whitish bloom. The canes grow up to {{convert|1.8|m|ft|abbr=on|frac=2}} long, usually arching but sometimes remaining straight. The canes have curved, sharp [[Thorns, spines, and prickles|thorns]],<ref name="marrone" /> while the [[Petiole (botany)|petioles]] and flower [[rachis]] have prickles.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=''Rubus occidentalis'' L.|url=http://www.ou.edu/biosurvey.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170303210605/http://biosurvey.ou.edu/shrub/rubu-occ.htm |archive-date=2017-03-03 |access-date=2026-06-15 |website=Oklahoma Biological Survey |publisher=[[University of Oklahoma]] |language=en-US}}</ref> The [[leaves]] are [[leaf shape|pinnate]], generally with five leaflets and strong-growing petioles in their first year, while leaves on flowering branchlets have three leaflets.{{Citation needed|date=June 2026}}

The flowers have long, slender [[sepal]]s {{convert|6 to 8|mm|frac=16|abbr=off}} long, more than twice as long as the [[petal]]s. The round [[aggregate fruit]], consisting of [[drupe]]lets, is {{convert|12 to 15|mm|frac=16|abbr=on}} in diameter<ref name=":0" /> and readily detaches from the carpel.<ref name="marrone" />

=== Similar species ===

The black raspberry is related to the red raspberries ''[[Rubus idaeus]]'' and ''[[Rubus strigosus|R. strigosus]]'',<ref name="grin" /><ref name="ncgr">{{cite web |title=Blackberry and Raspberry Genetic Resources - Rubus Germplasm - Rubus Genebank |url=https://www.ars.usda.gov/pacific-west-area/corvallis-or/national-clonal-germplasm-repository/docs/ncgr-corvallis-rubus-germplasm/ |publisher=National Clonal Germplasm Repository, US Department of Agriculture |access-date=19 July 2025 |location=Corvallis, Oregon |date=3 September 2020}}</ref> sharing the white underside of leaves<ref name="Brandeis">{{cite web |last1=Barotz |first1=Sharon |last2=Bilodeau |first2=Carrie |title=Black Raspberry |url=http://www.bio.brandeis.edu/fieldbio/medicinal_plants/pages/Black_raspberry.html |website=Medicinal Plants of the Northeast |publisher=[[Brandeis University]] |access-date=2 July 2021}}</ref> and fruit that easily detaches from the carpel.<ref name="marrone" />

It is also closely related to ''[[Rubus leucodermis|R. leucodermis]]'', which is also named black raspberry and blackcap.<ref name="grin" /><ref name="ncgr" /><ref name="finn">{{cite web |vauthors=Finn C, Strik B, Moore PP |title=Raspberry cultivars for the Pacific Northwest |url=https://extension.oregonstate.edu/catalog/pnw-655-raspberry-cultivars-pacific-northwest |publisher=Oregon State University Extension Service |access-date=19 July 2025 |date=2024}}</ref>

== Distribution and habitat ==

The plant is native to eastern North America, with a range as far east as [[New Brunswick]], as far west as [[Nebraska]], as far north as [[Quebec]], and as far south as [[Mississippi]].<ref name="grin" /><ref>{{Cite web|date=15 December 2014|title=Rubus distribution; see map for occidentalis |url=https://bonap.net/Napa/TaxonMaps/Genus/County/Rubus|publisher=The Biota of North America Program|access-date=19 July 2025}}</ref> It grows in disturbed areas, especially those that are logged or cut. It is also found in meadows, and near streams and lakes, trails or roadways.<ref name=marrone/>

== Ecology ==
The plants can be infested by [[apple mosaic virus]], [[black raspberry necrosis virus]], ''[[Elsinoë veneta]]'', [[raspberry bushy dwarf virus]], raspberry leaf curl virus, ''[[Rhizobium radiobacter]]'', ''[[Rhizobium rhizogenes]]'', ''[[Didymella applanata]]'', ''[[Monilinia fructigena]]'', ''[[Peronospora sparsa]]'', and ''[[Peridroma saucia]]''.<ref name=ncgr/><ref name=finn/><ref name="cabi">{{Cite web|title=''Rubus occidentalis'', black raspberry|url=https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/48009|date=19 November 2019|accessdate=11 August 2021|website=CABI Invasive Species Compendium}}</ref>

The plants provide cover and the berries are eaten by various birds and mammals.<ref name=":0" />

== Cultivation ==
A center for black raspberry cultivation is in the [[Willamette Valley]] of Oregon.<ref name="finn" /> The main [[cultivar]] is 'Munger'.<ref name="grin" /><ref name="finn" /> Other cultivars include 'Allen', 'Blackhawk', 'Bristol', 'Cumberland', 'Dundee', 'Hanover', 'Huron', 'Jewel', 'John Robertson', 'Logan', 'Macblack', 'Morrison', 'Munger', and 'Plum Farmer'.<ref name="ncgr" /><ref name="finn" /><ref>{{Cite web|date=8 November 2021|title=Raspberry varieties (includes black raspberries)|url=https://harvesttotable.com/raspberry_varieties_there_are/|publisher=Harvest to Table|accessdate=11 August 2021}}</ref> The plants are summer tipped by hand, mechanically pruned in winter and then machine harvested.<ref name="finn" /> The yields are generally low per acre and this is why the fruits are often expensive.

The species has been used in the breeding of many ''Rubus'' [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrids]]; those between red and black raspberries are common under the name purple raspberries; 'Brandywine', 'Royalty', and 'Estate' are examples of purple raspberry cultivars.<ref name=finn/> Wild purple raspberries have also been found in various places in northeastern North America where the two parental species co-occur and occasionally hybridize naturally.{{cn|date=June 2025}}

[[File:Black raspberries in a basket, side view.jpg|thumb|A [[punnet]] of black raspberries]]
== Uses ==

The berries are edible raw and can be made into jams and jellies.<ref name=":0" /> They have a high content of [[anthocyanin]]s.<ref name="genome">{{cite journal |vauthors=VanBuren R, Bryant D, Bushakra JM, et al. |title=The genome of black raspberry (''Rubus occidentalis'') |journal=The Plant Journal|volume=87 |issue=6 |pages=535–47 |date=September 2016 |pmid=27228578 |doi=10.1111/tpj.13215 |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/tpj.13215 }}</ref>

The berries are typically dried or frozen, made into [[purée]]s and juices, or processed as [[colorant]]s. Fresh berries are also marketed in season. Two [[liqueur]]s using black raspberry fruit include France's [[Chambord Liqueur Royale de France]] and various kinds of South Korea's [[Bokbunja-ju]].{{cn|date=July 2025}}
